title: Stately, plump Buck Mulligan came from the stairhead, bearing a bowl of lather on which a mirror and a razor lay crossed. A yellow dressinggown, ungirdled, was sustained gently behind him on the mild morning air. He held the bowl aloft and intoned:
html_source:
Buck Mulligan is modelled after Oliver St. John Gogarty, a fellow Irish poet.

This opening scene is a parody of the Catholic Mass suggested here by the “stately” manner of Buck’s entry, which follows that of a priest or clergyman, and again with the “cross(ing)” of the mirror and the razor. The bowl in the scene, “held aloft” ceremoniously, stands in for the chalice of communion that contains the blood of Christ.

It’s significant that the first word of Joyce’s novel, ‘Stately’ contains its last, ‘Yes’. This is a story of return, and as we depart, we have the shadow of our destination in mind.

The yellow dressinggown: 16 June is the feast day of St. John Francis Regis (1597-1640), the appropriate vestments for a Mass would be white and gold. Within the church the colour yellow suggests degradation, jealousy, treason and deceit. As such Judas is often portrayed in a garment of yellow.

The ungirdled gown is in contrast of the priests vow of chastity and the “razor” refers to slaughter, with Mulligan, the priest, acting as a butcher.
